pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–11 years

- **Topic:** Fair testing (engineering / prototype improvement)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Working Scientifically + Design & Technology):** draws on the WS requirement to set up "comparative and fair tests" and to use "results to… suggest improvements", combined with the D&T 'evaluate' strand — pupils "evaluate their ideas and products against… design criteria" and improve their work. This topic applies fair-test discipline specifically to testing a MODEL or PROTOTYPE, finding its failure points, and iterating.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 + ETS1 Engineering Design, grades 3–5):** SEP 3 at 3–5 requires planning and conducting investigations "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]." The engineering-design core idea 3-5-ETS1-3 is the direct match: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]" — essentially the verbatim topic description.

- **Operational details:** Builds on generating and comparing candidate solutions (prerequisite mt_HveO1bOXpJ). The child fair-tests a prototype (a bridge, a parachute, a boat) by holding all conditions constant except the one design feature under test, observes WHERE and HOW it fails (the failure point), proposes a specific improvement targeting that failure, and retests — the test→fail→improve→retest engineering loop. The fair-test rigour matters because otherwise an 'improvement' cannot be credited to the change. Feeds forward to planning enquiries with variable control (dependent mt_ArVBEpMAPk).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete, moving toward systematic). A learner who can plan a controlled test of a prototype with the right variable held constant, identify the specific failure point from the results, and propose and retest a targeted improvement has met the bar.
bestPractices: Frame testing as diagnosis, not verdict: the goal is to locate the SPECIFIC failure point (where/why it broke), not just to record pass/fail — this turns a test into information that drives the next design change.

Insist on controlled comparison when crediting an improvement: change only the one design feature between prototype versions so any performance gain can be attributed to that change, not to an incidental difference.
Make iteration explicit and expected: run the test→identify failure→improve→retest loop at least twice so pupils experience redesign as normal engineering rather than as 'getting it wrong'.
Tie every proposed improvement to evidence from the test ('it snapped in the middle, so I'll add a support there'), not to untested hunches or decoration.
Quantify where possible (mass held, distance travelled, drop time) and take repeat trials so a fragile prototype's result isn't judged on a single fluke run.
keyRepresentations: The test → identify failure point → improve → retest iteration loop
A prototype annotated with its observed failure point (where it bent/broke/leaked)
A version-comparison table (v1 vs v2) with the single changed feature and the measured outcome
Design criteria + constraints checklist the prototype is tested against
A repeat-trials results strip for one prototype version
commonMisconceptions: Treating a test as a pass/fail verdict rather than as diagnostic information about where and why the design failed.
Changing several design features at once between versions, then not knowing which change produced the improvement (loss of fair-test control).
Believing a first failure means the design (or the designer) is 'wrong', rather than that iteration is the normal engineering process.
Proposing improvements based on appearance or preference instead of on the observed failure point.
Judging a prototype on a single trial, ignoring that variability needs repeat runs to see the real behaviour.

learn.summary: For ages 8–11, learners run the engineering test→find failure point→improve→retest loop on a prototype (bridge, parachute, boat). The core skill is controlled fair testing of a model: hold every condition constant except the one design feature being changed, locate the SPECIFIC point where and why it fails, propose an improvement targeted at that failure, and retest under identical conditions so any gain can be credited to the change. Hands-on building and testing is the primary vehicle (consistent with the KS2/NGSS requirement for pupils to build, test and improve); build-and-test simulations, a 3D structure sandbox, a reference diagram, recognition checks and a design-mentor dialogue serve as distinct supports with their own purposes and limits.

activities.title: Build, test, and diagnose the failure point of a prototype
feedback: If a learner records only 'it broke' or 'pass/fail', prompt: 'Where exactly did it fail, and why do you think it failed there?' Diagnosis drives the next change.
If the retest uses gentler loading or a different position, note that the before/after comparison is no longer fair — hold the loading method identical so any difference is down to the design.
If several features change at once in version 2, point out you can no longer tell which change helped; change one thing aimed at the observed failure.
If the improvement targets a part that wasn't failing (or is decorative), redirect: identify the actual failure point first, then target it.

If a learner just keeps tweaking until it holds without naming what failed or measuring the change, redirect: name the failure and compare against the design criteria — the aim is to learn WHY it failed, not only to get it to hold.
Reinforce that a first failure is normal engineering, not 'getting it wrong' — expect to run the loop at least twice.
activities.rationale: The objective is iterative, controlled testing of a prototype with evidence-driven redesign. Physical building and testing lets learners observe real failure modes and run genuine before/after comparisons, matching the fair-test and evaluate-and-improve standards.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Working Scientifically requires setting up comparative and fair tests and using results to suggest improvements; D&T requires evaluating products against design criteria and improving work.
NGSS 3-5-ETS1-3 requires planning and carrying [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4].
learnerActions: Build a simple prototype against stated design criteria — e.g. a paper bridge spanning the gap between two tables, a parachute, or a floating boat.

Plan a fair test: decide one loading/testing method and keep it fixed (same weight increments, same position, same drop height), and agree that version 2 will change only one design feature, chosen after you see where and how version 1 fails.

Run the test and observe carefully WHERE and HOW it fails — e.g. 'it sagged and tore in the middle', 'the seam leaked at the corner', 'it buckled near the left support'. Record this failure point, not just pass/fail.
Propose one specific improvement aimed squarely at that failure point (e.g. 'it snapped in the middle, so I'll add a support there' or 'fold the middle to stiffen it').
Build version 2 changing only that one feature, then retest under identical conditions, and judge from the results whether it actually improved.
activities.intendedInsight: A test is a diagnosis, not a verdict: it shows where and how the design failed, giving evidence for reasoning about why, so you know what to change. Changing only one feature between versions, while keeping test conditions identical, is what lets you credit an improvement to that change (repeat trials then check it was not a fluke).

activities.title: Repeat trials and quantify before crediting an improvement
feedback: If a learner declares 'it's stronger' after one run, ask whether a second or third run would hold up — one trial can be a fluke.
If no numbers are recorded, prompt them to measure (mass, distance, time) so before/after can actually be compared.
Praise tables that pin the single changed feature next to its measured outcome — that is what makes the comparison fair and readable.
activities.rationale: Quantifying and repeating trials guards against crediting the design change with a performance difference that is really due to run-to-run variability, supporting the fair-test discipline. No recorded source claim states the repeat-trials/number-of-trials principle directly, so none is cited.
learnerActions: For one prototype version, run the same test several times (repeat trials), using a fresh identical copy whenever the test destroys the prototype, and record the measured outcome each time — mass held, distance travelled, drop time.
Compare the repeat results: notice whether a single run was a fluke or whether the behaviour is consistent.
Fill in a version-comparison table: v1 vs v2, the single changed feature, and the measured outcome for each, with repeat trials for each version.
Decide whether version 2 is genuinely better given the spread of results, not just one lucky run.
activities.intendedInsight: A fragile prototype's result shouldn't be judged on a single run; repeat trials and measurement reveal the real behaviour and make an 'improvement' claim trustworthy.

activities.title: Build-and-test simulation with a locked version tray (supporting scaffold)
feedback: Use the stress/where-it-broke overlay to answer 'why did it fail there?' before changing anything.
Let the locked version tray enforce the fair comparison, but have learners state in words which single feature changed so the control is explicit, not just automatic.

Treat a surviving retest as evidence, within the simulation's model, that the targeted change helped, and check it against a physical test where possible — ask what would happen if two features had changed at once.
activities.rationale: A recomputing build-and-test sandbox can surface failure points and enforce a locked fair comparison across versions quickly; it is a strong support alongside, not a replacement for, hands-on building, which also builds material intuition. Its proposed advantages are not established by the sources, so no source claim is cited here.
learnerActions: In a bridge/parachute/boat builder with a test rig, assemble a prototype and load/drop/float it under fixed conditions.
When it fails, read the overlay that highlights the exact failure point (the beam that buckles, the seam that leaks) and name where and why it failed.
Use a version tray that keeps v1 beside v2 and locks all conditions except the one feature you change; reinforce precisely the highlighted failure point and retest.
Watch whether the prototype survives the identical retest, and connect that result to the single change you made.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the exact failure point highlighted and retesting under locked identical conditions can make 'test as diagnosis' and 'controlled comparison' visible and fast to iterate.

activities.title: 3D structure sandbox for inherently spatial failure modes (alternative)
feedback: Only reach for the 3D view when the failure mode is inherently spatial; for a simple side-on break a 2D bench or physical model is just as clear.
Still change one feature at a time and keep test conditions identical — the fair-test discipline is unchanged in 3D.
activities.rationale: Structural prototypes can have spatial failure modes, so a 3D sandbox may add value when the weakness is inherently three-dimensional; this is offered as an alternative with a stated affordance, not a universal requirement.
learnerActions: For a structure whose failure is genuinely three-dimensional (buckling, twisting, toppling of a bridge, tower or parachute), build it in a 3D builder with physics and load it.
Observe how it deforms and fails in three dimensions, which a flat side view might hide.
Target the spatial weakness (e.g. add bracing against twist), then retest under identical conditions.
activities.intendedInsight: Some failure modes are spatial, so viewing deformation in three dimensions can reveal a weakness that a single 2D view may not show.

activities.title: Recognition checks and design-mentor dialogue (recognition and justification supports)
feedback: Use the recognition items to surface the misconception that changing several features is still a fair test — flag any option where more than one feature differs.
In the mentor dialogue, push every improvement back to the observed failure ('it buckled here, so…'), rejecting answers based on appearance or preference.
Note that these recognition and discussion tasks check and sharpen reasoning; they do not by themselves generate the test evidence or elicit the hands-on build.
activities.rationale: Recognition items assess understanding of fair comparison and the evidence→improvement link, and a mentor persona can press for evidence-based justification; both complement but do not substitute for running the actual tests, since recognition alone does not elicit production.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-5-ETS1-3 requires planning and carrying [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4].
learnerActions: Answer a multiple-choice item: 'Which version comparison is a fair test?' (only one design feature differs between versions and the test conditions are identical).
Match observed failure points to the improvement that targets each one.
Put the test–improve–retest steps into the correct order.
After testing, defend your change to a design-mentor who asks 'what's your evidence that this will fix it?' and justify the improvement from the test observation.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can check that they recognise fair comparisons, the evidence→improvement link and the iteration loop, and can articulate the reasoning behind a change — though recognising a fair test is not the same as producing one at the bench.

constraints: Builds on generating and comparing candidate solutions; learners should already be able to propose more than one design idea before fair-testing one.

Credit an improvement only under controlled comparison: change exactly one design feature between versions and keep loading method, position, increments and conditions identical, or any gain cannot be attributed to the change.
Run the loop at least twice so redesign is experienced as normal engineering, not as failure.
Tie every proposed improvement to an observed failure point, not to appearance, preference or decoration.
Recognition and sequencing items and the mentor dialogue check reasoning but do not elicit independent construction or generate test evidence; keep an actual build-and-test as the primary task.

A static annotated diagram can label a failure point for reference but, because it does not recompute, cannot show the retest outcome needed for iterative controlled testing; use it only as a reference aid.
The 3D sandbox is justified when the failure mode is inherently spatial; for simple breaks a 2D bench or physical model is equally clear and cheaper.
Feeds forward to planning enquiries with variable control.

Checkpoint: a learner meets the bar by planning a controlled prototype test with the right variable held constant, identifying the specific failure point from results, and proposing and retesting a targeted improvement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted a live 2D sandbox is 'the only medium' that can deliver failure-point observation and fair-test comparison. This overstates necessity: hands-on physical building and testing also delivers both, so the simulation is presented here as a strong support rather than the sole viable medium.

The legacy claim that a non-recomputing image 'cannot support' the learning was scoped: a static diagram cannot show recomputed retest results for iteration but can still label a failure point as a reference.

Activity 2 (repeat trials / quantification) has sourceClaims set to []: the principle is grounded in the pedagogy summary's SEP 3 paraphrase ('number of trials considered') and bestPractices, but neither exact sources[].claim string mentions repeat trials, so no claim directly supports that rationale.

Activity 3 (build-and-test sim) has sourceClaims set to []: its distinctive principle is the sim's visualization/iteration-speed affordance, which the rationale itself states is not source-established. The underlying fair-test/failure-point principle remains cited in Activity 1 where it is directly taught.

One source (NGSS 3-5-ETS1-3, Appendix F) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its citation strength accordingly. The DfE source is marked verified:true. No fresh verification was performed in this rewrite.

probeDeeper: Where exactly did it fail, and why do you think it failed there?
What one change did you make, and how is it aimed at that weakness?
If you added the weights more slowly the second time, could you still say your new design is stronger? Why not?
How will you keep the test fair so you can trust that the improvement is real?
assess.correctAnswer: The child loads the bridge in a controlled way (same position, same weight increments), identifies the specific failure point and why it fails (e.g. it sags and tears in the middle), makes a targeted change aimed at that weakness (e.g. folds or beams the middle), and retests under identical conditions so the before/after comparison is fair — then judges whether it actually improved.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unfair retest: loads the improved bridge more gently, or in a different spot, so 'it's better' isn't a fair claim.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold the loading method identical between runs; only the design should change, so any difference is down to the design.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The retest conditions differ from the first test — different loading position, increments, or method.

errorPatterns.pattern: Untargeted improvement: reinforces a part that wasn't failing, or changes several things at once so the effect of any one is unclear.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the actual failure point first, then change one thing aimed squarely at it before retesting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The improve step isn't linked to the observed failure point, or bundles multiple changes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Make-it-work instead of find-out: keeps tweaking until it holds without noting what caused the failure or measuring the change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the failure, measure the load before and after, and compare against the design criteria — test to learn, not just to succeed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No failure analysis or before/after data — the goal has slid from testing to just getting it to work.

responseLevels.gap: Tinkers until it works without identifying the failure point, or retests under different conditions so any improvement can't be judged.
responseLevels.full: Runs a controlled test, pinpoints the specific failure and why it occurs, makes a targeted improvement, and retests under identical conditions to judge the change fairly — coordinating design, evidence, and fair comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies a failure point and makes an improvement, but the retest isn't fully controlled, or the change isn't clearly targeted at the observed weakness.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a paper bridge you've built spanning two tables, and some weights. Plan and run a fair test to find out how much it holds, spot where and why it fails, then make one improvement and test again to see if it's better. Keep the test fair each time. I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates engineering-with-evidence — controlled loading, a change aimed at the observed failure, a fair before/after comparison — from trial and error: changing the test conditions between runs (so improvement can't be attributed), or 'fixing' a part that wasn't the problem.
